h1: A brewpub in a tech park and the weekday trade it relies on
title: A Brewpub in a Tech Park: Weekday Trade | Craft Beer School
desc: What a brewpub in a tech park must earn from lunch, after-work and corporate bookings, plus the questions to settle before you sign a lease.
teaser: A tech park gives a brewpub thousands of possible customers Monday to Friday. It also gives you an empty room on Saturday night.
standfirst: A brewpub near an office cluster lives on weekday footfall. That is a different business from one built on weekend leisure. Here is how to plan the trade, the menu and the beer for it.
sections: A weekday business with a weekend problem

Tech parks in Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad and Chennai pack many thousands of workers into a small area. On paper that is a very strong customer base. In practice the crowd arrives at nine, eats at one, leaves around six and, in many parks, does not come back until Monday.

So the brewpub earns most of its money in a few windows: the lunch hour, the early evening and the occasional team event. The rest of the week has to be planned around those windows. If your pour cost, rent and staff are sized for a Saturday night crowd that never turns up, you will feel it in the first quarter.

Before you commit to a site, count the real weekday footfall and the number of offices within a ten minute walk. Ask for the park's own rules too. Some parks restrict alcohol on the premises. Some have security gates that shape who can reach you. Many work patterns are also shifting towards hybrid. Do not assume a full office on every day.

Lunch. Time is the constraint. Office workers have an hour, often less. A lunch menu that lands in fifteen minutes will do better than a long one. Beer is usually a small share of lunch sales near offices, so treat the lunch as a food business first and a beer business second. Offer low-strength and non-alcoholic options.

After work. The window from about five to eight is where a brewpub earns its margin. Team outings, farewells and quick drinks before the commute home all land here. Fast service, a short list of reliable beers and food that comes out hot matter more than range.

Events. Booked team dinners, product launches and offsites are the best revenue a tech-park brewpub can win. They are planned, they are large and they can fill a quiet night. Build a simple events pack: a set menu, a beer flight option and a price per head. Our guide to filling a brewpub on slow weekday nights goes deeper on the evening side.
Design the beer list for the hour

A tech-park crowd is mixed. Some people want a familiar lager, some want to try something new and some do not drink alcohol at all. A list of four to six beers usually serves that spread: a crisp lager or pilsner, a wheat beer, a pale ale, one seasonal and one low-strength option.

Keep the core beers consistent. Office workers who return every week want the same beer to taste the same. Consistency is a brewing discipline: temperature control, yeast handling and clean lines. A brewpub that sells a good beer on Tuesday and a different one on Thursday will lose its regulars.

Remember that the brewhouse floor can only follow demand so far. A lager needs several weeks in tank. If your weekday volume jumps, you cannot brew your way out of it overnight, so keep a buffer of the best sellers.

A brewpub licence is state-specific. Rules on where a brewpub may stand, the hours it may serve, the distance from certain buildings and the annual costs vary by state and change often. Some tech parks are inside special economic zones or private campuses with their own conditions on top.

Work with a licensing adviser and read the current notification for your state before you sign a lease. Our guide to trade licence and shop registration steps for a brewpub sets out the general process. It is not legal advice. The details are yours to check.
Test the numbers before the lease

Build a simple weekday model with hypothetical figures first, then replace them with your own. For example, suppose the brewpub sees 60 covers at lunch, 80 in the evening and 4 events a month. Multiply by your average spend per head, subtract the cost of food and beer, then subtract rent, staff and utilities. If the month does not clear, change the model, not the optimism.

Look at the weekend separately. If the park is empty, can you earn enough from a smaller weekend opening, a family brunch or private bookings? Or is it better to close and save the staff cost? Our comparison of brewpub or microbrewery helps if the weekday trade looks too thin to carry a full pub.

A brewer can design a good beer and still lose money here, because the failure is in the cash flow, not the recipe. Matching footfall to staffing, pricing to the lunch crowd and brew schedule to peaks is a business skill. It rarely appears in a brewing course and it is what separates a busy pub from a quiet one.
faqs: Is a tech park a good place for a brewpub?
It can be, if the weekday footfall is real and the park permits alcohol. Count actual visitors and nearby offices. Plan for quiet weekends.
What sells best to office crowds?
A short list of reliable beers, fast food and a low-strength option. Booked team events usually bring the best revenue.
Do I need a different licence near a tech park?
Brewpub licences are state-specific and the park may add its own rules. Check the current notification and work with a licensing adviser.
Should a tech-park brewpub open on weekends?
Only if the numbers support it. Compare the extra income from brunch or private events with the added staff and utility cost.
